passages.t: Defeat at Ai, and Joshua on his face
passages.happening:
The chapter begins by telling the reader a secret. “The Israelites, however, acted unfaithfully regarding the things devoted to destruction. Achan son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of what was set apart. So the anger of the LORD burned against the Israelites” (verse 1).

Joshua knows none of this. He sends scouts up from Jericho to the next town, Ai. They come back confident: ‘two or three thousand men are enough’ (verse 3). About three thousand go up. They run from the men of Ai, and about thirty-six of them are killed. “So the hearts of the people melted and became like water” (verse 5).

Joshua tears his clothes and falls face down before the ark until evening, with the elders beside him and dust on their heads (verse 6). Then he prays. “O, Lord GOD,” Joshua said, “why did You ever bring this people across the Jordan to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be destroyed?” (verse 7). He fears that the peoples of the land will hear and wipe Israel out. He ends with a question: “Then what will You do for Your great name?” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Ai lay in the hills above Jericho, near Bethel, on the road into the heart of the land. Its name means ‘the ruin’. Where exactly it stood is debated. The mound most often identified with it was empty in the period when Israel would have come, and scholars have answered that in several ways. The book page sets them out and takes no side.

The writer lets the reader know about Achan before anyone in the story does. Everything that follows is read with that knowledge, and it is painful to watch. The scouts are sure of themselves. No one asks God. Men climb a hill expecting an easy day.

Thirty-six dead was a small loss for an army. The damage was to Israel's heart. In chapter 2 Rahab had said that the hearts of the Canaanites were melting. In chapter 5 the kings' hearts melted. Now the same words are used of Israel. The fear has changed sides.

Tearing the clothes, lying face down and putting dust on the head were the customs of mourning. Joshua and the elders grieve as people grieve for the dead.

His prayer is not a model of calm faith. He sounds like the generation that died in the wilderness, which had wished it had never left Egypt. He even says, ‘If only we had been content to stay on the other side of the Jordan’. The Bible lets its leaders pray like this, and it does not hide it. But one thing in the prayer is sound. Joshua's last thought is for God's name, for what the nations will conclude about the LORD if his people are destroyed. Moses had prayed in the same way after the golden calf.

Verse 1 says that ‘the Israelites’ acted unfaithfully, though one man took the goods. That way of speaking is strange to modern readers. Israel was bound to God as one people under one covenant, and what one member did in secret touched everyone. The thirty-six who died had stolen nothing.
passages.later:
Chronicles remembers the man by a changed name that carries the story in it: “The son of Carmi: Achar, who brought trouble upon Israel by violating the ban on devoted things” (1 Chronicles 2:7).

Paul uses a homely picture for the way one person's hidden sin affects a whole community: “Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?” (1 Corinthians 5:6).
passages.asks: The scouts said that a few men would be enough, and no one asked God. Ask what you have treated as small enough to handle without praying. Then look at Joshua on the ground. Ask whether you bring your defeats to God in plain words, even angry ones, or only your thanks. And ask whether there is anything hidden in your own life that others are paying for.

passages.happening:
God's answer is abrupt. “Stand up! Why have you fallen on your face? Israel has sinned; they have transgressed My covenant that I commanded them, and they have taken some of what was devoted to destruction. Indeed, they have stolen and lied, and they have put these things with their own possessions” (verses 10-11).

That is why Israel ran. By keeping what was under the ban, Israel has come under the ban. “I will no longer be with you unless you remove from among you whatever is devoted to destruction” (verse 12).

God tells Joshua what to do. The people are to consecrate themselves. In the morning they will come forward tribe by tribe, then clan by clan, then family by family, then man by man. The one who is found with the devoted things is to be burned, with all that belongs to him (verses 13-15).

Joshua rises early. The tribe of Judah is taken. Then the clan of the Zerahites. Then the family of Zabdi. And then, man by man, “Achan son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was selected” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
God does not answer Joshua's question about why he brought Israel over the river. He tells him to get up. Prayer was not what the moment required. There was something to put right, and lying on the ground would not do it.

God names what happened with a pile of verbs: sinned, transgressed, taken, stolen, lied, hidden. A theft of a few objects is called a breach of the covenant. The goods were not just valuable. They had been given over to God, and taking them was taking from him.

The warning of chapter 6 has come true word for word. Joshua had said that anyone who took devoted things would set the camp of Israel apart for destruction. Jericho was under the ban, and now Israel is. The same judgment that fell on a Canaanite city is turned on God's own people. The book will not let Israel think the ban was a weapon that pointed only outward.

The words ‘I will no longer be with you’ are the most frightening in the chapter. Everything since chapter 1 has rested on the promise, ‘I will be with you’. The commander of the LORD's army had told Joshua that God was on neither side by right. This chapter shows what that means in practice. God's presence with Israel is not a possession Israel holds whatever it does.

The text does not say how the choice was made each time. It was probably by lot, the way Israel asked God to decide a matter. Israel was organized in nested groups, tribe, clan, family and household, and the search moves down through them one step at a time.

The slowness is part of the story. Achan stands in the crowd through all of it. He watches his tribe taken, then his clan, then his family. At every step he could have come forward. He waits until his own name is called.
passages.later:
The Psalms know what it is to stay silent about sin: “When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3). And they know the other way: “Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity” (Psalm 32:5).

Proverbs puts the same thing in one line: “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).
passages.asks: Achan stood silent while the circle closed around him, step by step. Ask whether there is something you are waiting to be caught in when you could come forward. Ask who you would tell. And think about what God said to Joshua: get up. Ask whether you are praying about something that God has already told you to deal with.

passages.happening:
Joshua speaks to Achan gently. “My son, give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make a confession to Him. I urge you to tell me what you have done; do not hide it from me” (verse 19).

Achan answers. “It is true,” Achan replied, “I have sinned against the LORD, the God of Israel” (verse 20). He says what he took: a fine cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold. ‘I coveted them and took them’ (verse 21). They are buried in the ground inside his tent.

Messengers run to the tent and find it all there. They bring the things out and spread them before the LORD (verses 22-23).

Then Joshua and all Israel take Achan, the silver, the cloak and the gold, his sons and daughters, his animals, his tent and all he has, to a valley. Joshua says, “Why have you brought this trouble upon us?” (verse 25). All Israel stones him. The verse goes on, ‘Then they stoned the others and burned their bodies’ (verse 25).

They raise a great heap of rocks over him. “So the LORD turned from His burning anger. Therefore that place is called the Valley of Achor to this day” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Joshua calls him ‘my son’. There is no rage in the scene. The words ‘give glory to the LORD’ were the form used to put a person on his honor to tell the truth, with God as witness.

Achan's confession traces the path of the sin in three steps: he saw, he coveted, he took. The story of the garden uses the same steps, when the woman saw the fruit, desired it and took it. ‘Covet’ is the word of the tenth commandment. The theft began as a look and a wish.

Shinar is the Bible's name for Babylonia, so the cloak was an expensive import. The silver and gold were real wealth. A shekel was a weight, a little under half an ounce. There were no coins yet.

There is a bitter irony here. At the very next city, Ai, God allows Israel to keep the plunder (8:2). Had Achan waited, he could have had such things with a clear conscience.

Stoning was carried out by the whole community. No single person was the executioner. The people together removed what had brought guilt on them all.

The place name is a play on words. The Hebrew verb for ‘bring trouble’ is akar, and Achor means ‘trouble’. Joshua had warned at Jericho that taking the devoted things would bring trouble on the camp.

This is a dreadful scene, and the Bible tells it without pleasure. A man is put to death by his own people, and the plain sense of the text is that his sons and daughters died with him. The hard question below takes that up. These notes do not defend it or explain it away.
passages.later:
The prophets did not leave this valley as it was. Through Hosea, God says of his unfaithful people, “There I will give back her vineyards and make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope” (Hosea 2:15). Isaiah sees it as a place of peace: ‘the Valley of Achor a resting place for herds, for My people who seek Me’ (Isaiah 65:10).

Paul writes of one who took on himself the curse that others had earned: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

And the New Testament holds out a promise to everyone who confesses: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
passages.hard:
Why did Achan's sons and daughters die with him? The law says, “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16).

The question is a real one, and the law quoted above is the reason it is. Readers have answered in several ways.

Some hold that the family must have known. The goods were buried under the floor of the family's own tent. On this view they shared in hiding the theft.

Some point to the law of the ban. This was not an ordinary court case. Whoever took what was devoted to destruction came under the same ban, with all that was his, as the law required for an Israelite town that turned to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:15-17).

Some point to the way the ancient world thought of a household, as a single body that stood or fell with its head.

Some note that the Hebrew of verse 25 is not fully clear about who was stoned and burned, though its plain sense includes the family.

These notes do not choose among these answers, and none of them takes the weight away. Many readers find that none fully satisfies. The text itself presents the day as extraordinary and terrible. And later Scripture insists that each person answers for his own sin: “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son” (Ezekiel 18:20).

The story lays down no rule for today. It gives no family, church or state any right to punish one person for what another has done.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Achan saw, wanted and took, and then buried it under his own floor. Ask what you have looked at long enough to want, and whether the wanting has started to make its own excuses. Ask what is buried under your floor. And then hear what the prophets said of this valley. God can make the place of a person's worst trouble ‘a gateway of hope’. Ask what it would mean to bring him yours.
